title: U.S. sanctions Canadian branch of Italian criminal organization, including funeral homes in Toronto area
summary: The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, an Italian Mafia group.

image.caption: The Vescio Funeral Home in Maple, Ont., is pictured in an undated handout image. (U.S. Treasury)

blocks.text: The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, an Italian Mafia group.
One of six prominent gang members serves as president of funeral homes in Woodbridge, Maple and Toronto
The United States on Thursday announced sanctions targeting what authorities described as the Canadian arm of the 'Ndrangheta, one of Italy's most powerful criminal organizations.

A statement from the U.S. Treasury said the enforcement targeted "a powerful transnational faction of the 'Ndrangheta" group in the Toronto area. That group has been involved in "drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, and other crimes," officials said.
The new sanctions target six people officials identified as key figures of the gang in the Toronto area, as well as the wife and children of one leader: Luigi Vescio Sr., 55.
Vescio Sr., who the statement says is known as "The Undertaker," serves as president of several funeral homes in Ontario, including:

items: Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Woodbridge, Ont.
Vescio Funeral Home (Maple) Inc. in Maple, Ont.
Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Toronto.

blocks.text: Described as a senior, Canadian-born member of the 'Ndrangheta, Vescio Sr. also controls a Toronto-based luxury limousine rental business: Phantom Limousine Services Inc. The businesses have now been sanctioned, as have members of his family.

His wife, Rose Vescio, and his two children, Luigi Vescio Jr. and Laura Vescio, were listed "for their roles in owning and operating the Vescio Funeral Homes" on Vescio Sr.'s behalf, the statement said.

blocks.text: Experts on the 'Ndrangheta have described the criminal syndicate as one of the most financially sophisticated in the West, with capital heavily invested in the world of finance and clan branches firmly ensconced around the globe, including in the Toronto and Montreal areas. Experts estimated the clans' annual income in 2021 would range from $50 billion to $85 billion a year.

The sanctions effectively cut off the people and businesses from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
The sanctions also targeted the Comancheros, one of the oldest biker gangs in Australia, also accused of running global drug trafficking operations.
